result: A single trypanosome is sufficient to establish productive tsetse fly infection. Experiments showed that on average, ingestion of just two stumpy parasites produced robust infections of tsetse midgut, proventriculus, and salivary glands. Even a single stumpy cell on average was sufficient to produce salivary gland infections in almost 5% of tsetse, and when reduced to 0.2 cells per bloodmeal, 0.9% of flies still acquired salivary gland infections.
evaluation: Claims C39, C52-C54, C80, and C117 are well-supported by systematic quantitative data presented in Figure 2A showing infection rates at various parasite doses. The experimental design includes appropriate controls (monomorphic parasites), multiple replicates, and clear dose-response relationships. The transmission index (TI) provides a validated measure of successful life cycle completion.

result: Slender stage trypanosomes can infect tsetse flies and complete the full developmental cycle with comparable or superior efficiency to stumpy stages. Slender parasites infected midgut, proventriculus, and salivary glands. When flies were fed with an average of two slender parasites, the transmission index (TI) was higher for slender cells (0.60) than stumpy cells (0.31). Even one slender parasite on average established infections with a TI of 0.44.
evaluation: Claims C40, C63-C68, C81, C118-C119, C149, and C151 are strongly supported by experimental data in Figures 2A, 2B, and 3. Multiple independent experiments with different slender cell preparations (including freshly differentiated cells from metacyclics, C68) demonstrate reproducibility. The higher TI for slender cells at low doses (C66, C76) is particularly compelling evidence challenging the traditional dogma.

result: SIF-induced and ES-induced stumpy parasites are equally efficient in completing the tsetse fly cycle. For flies infected with two trypanosomes on average, the TI was comparable between SIF-induced (0.29) and ES-induced (0.31) stumpy trypanosomes, with a similar TI of 0.23 observed for flies ingesting one trypanosome on average.
evaluation: Claims C56-C58 and C62 are supported by quantitative data in Figures 2A and 3 comparing the two stumpy induction methods. The comparable TI values demonstrate that the ES-attenuation method produces functionally equivalent stumpy cells to SIF induction, validating this experimental approach and ruling out method-specific artifacts.

result: Monomorphic trypanosomes can establish midgut infections but cannot complete the developmental cycle. No salivary gland infections were observed with monomorphic cells even at high doses, but even two monomorphic slender parasites could establish midgut infection. This demonstrates that midgut infection is independent of developmental competence and does not require the stumpy stage.
evaluation: Claims C70-C73 are supported by control experiments with monomorphic parasites (Figure 2A, rows xiii-xv). The ability of monomorphic cells to establish midgut but not salivary gland infections provides important negative controls demonstrating that initial survival in the midgut is distinct from developmental progression. This challenges previous assumptions about selective elimination of slender parasites (C73).

result: Stumpy stages appear more effective at establishing initial midgut infections, while slender-derived parasites produce salivary gland infections more efficiently (higher TI). SIF-induced stumpy cells showed higher midgut infection rates than slender counterparts, but infections with one to two slender cells produced higher TI values than stumpy cells.
evaluation: Claims C74-C77, C120-C121 are supported by comparative data in Figures 2A-B and Figure 3. The differential performance at midgut establishment versus progression to salivary glands is an important nuanced finding. However, the interpretation (C77) that slender cells have "at least comparable overall developmental competence" is reasonable given the higher TI values, though the biological mechanism remains speculative.

result: In the tsetse midgut, slender trypanosomes activate the PAD1 pathway and differentiate to procyclic stage without cell cycle arrest. As early as 2 hr post-infection, 0.8% of dividing (2K1N) slender cells showed PAD1 signal. By 8 hr, 50.4% were PAD1-positive, reaching 91.8% by 48 hr. Remarkably, at 15 hr post-infection, the majority of replicating cells were PAD1-positive with no indication of cell cycle arrest.
evaluation: Claims C6, C83-C90, and C97 are strongly supported by in vivo time-course data in Figures 5A-B and Figure 6. The observation of PAD1-positive dividing cells (C87) is particularly important, directly demonstrating that PAD1 activation occurs without cell cycle arrest. The large sample sizes (n=1845 slender cells) and multiple timepoints provide robust evidence. Statistical modeling (GAM) appropriately accounts for temporal dynamics.

result: Stumpy trypanosomes remain cell cycle-arrested for the first day after tsetse uptake, then differentiate to procyclic cells. Stumpy cells remained as 1K1N cells in cell cycle arrest for the first day, started expressing EP1:YFP after 4 hr (16.2% by 10 hr), and re-entered the cell cycle after 2 days. EP1:YFP expression in slender parasites lagged 12 hr behind stumpy cells, but differentiation kinetics were comparable.
evaluation: Claims C91-C93, C95-C96 are supported by in vivo time-course data in Figures 5C and 6 (n=1237 stumpy cells). The delayed cell cycle re-entry in stumpy cells contrasts with continuous division in slender cells, highlighting a key mechanistic difference. The observation that EP expression precedes cell cycle re-entry (C93) is consistent with prior literature (C94) and validates the experimental approach.

result: PAD1 pathway activation is essential for differentiation to procyclic stage, while cell cycle arrest is not. The observation that slender cells differentiate without cell cycle arrest, and that EP1 surface expression correlates with PAD1 activation in both cell types, strongly suggests PAD1 is essential but cell cycle arrest is dispensable.
evaluation: Claims C98, C115, and C150 represent key mechanistic inferences well-supported by the combined in vivo data (Figures 5-6). The logic is sound: if slender cells can differentiate while dividing (C90) but always activate PAD1 first (C97), then PAD1 is necessary but cell cycle arrest is not. The correlation between PAD1 activation and EP1 surface access (C115) provides additional mechanistic support.

result: In vitro differentiation experiments confirm that slender trypanosomes can directly differentiate to procyclic stage without cell cycle arrest. Upon cis-aconitate treatment, slender cells rapidly activated PAD1 (83.2% by 10 hr, peaking at 98.3% by 24 hr), followed by EP1 expression (19.6% by 8 hr, 98.3% by 3 days). PAD1-positive slender cells continued dividing throughout differentiation, establishing a proliferating procyclic population by 3 days.
evaluation: Claims C104-C108 and C113 are supported by in vitro time-course data in Figures 7A-B, 8, and morphological analysis (Figure 7 supplement 3). The in vitro results (n=1653 slender cells) corroborate the in vivo findings, demonstrating that the phenomenon is not specific to the tsetse midgut environment. The continuous presence of PAD1-positive dividing cells (C107) directly parallels the in vivo observations, strengthening the overall conclusion.

result: In vitro, stumpy parasites rapidly express EP1 but remain cell cycle-arrested initially. Stumpy cells responded to cis-aconitate with rapid EP1:YFP expression (28.6% by 2 hr, 96.7% by 24 hr) but were not dividing during the first day. Cell cycle re-entry began only after 15 hr, with normal procyclic cell cycle profile not reached until day 3.
evaluation: Claims C109-C112 are supported by in vitro data in Figures 7C and 8 (n=1798 stumpy cells). These results parallel the in vivo stumpy differentiation kinetics, demonstrating consistency between experimental systems. The delayed cell cycle re-entry contrasts with the continuous division of slender cells, reinforcing the key mechanistic difference between the two pathways.

result: The overall developmental capacity of slender and stumpy cells is comparable both in vitro and in vivo.
evaluation: Claim C116 is a summary conclusion well-supported by the combined in vivo (Figures 5-6) and in vitro (Figures 7-8) differentiation data. Both cell types successfully differentiate to procyclic stage with similar kinetics (though different mechanisms), and both can complete the full tsetse life cycle (Figures 2-3). This represents a major conceptual advance in understanding trypanosome biology.

result: EP1 expression does not directly correlate with acquisition of procyclic morphology. At 24 hr in vivo, only 9.8% of slender cells were EP1-positive, but EP1-negative cells frequently exhibited procyclic morphology.
evaluation: Claims C99-C100 are supported by observations in Figures 4 and 6. This finding suggests that morphological changes can precede EP1 surface expression, possibly due to earlier expression of GPEET (C101). However, the manuscript acknowledges that GPEET expression was not directly assessed, representing a limitation. The observation is consistent with prior work showing uncoupling of EP expression from differentiation commitment (C94).

result: The findings demonstrate greater plasticity in the trypanosome life cycle than previously supposed, challenging the rigid view of the process.
evaluation: Claims C9, C41, C157-C158 represent high-level conclusions well-supported by the experimental findings. The demonstration that slender cells can complete the life cycle (C7, C40, C119) and differentiate without cell cycle arrest (C90, C113) directly contradicts the traditional rigid model requiring stumpy stage formation. This represents a paradigm shift in understanding trypanosome transmission biology.

result: The findings may provide a solution to the transmission paradox—the successful transmission of parasites in chronic infections despite low parasitemia—without challenging existing work on stumpy trypanosomes.
evaluation: Claims C10, C148, and C159 represent speculative interpretations about field implications. While the demonstration that single slender cells can infect flies (C39, C80) provides a plausible mechanism for transmission at low parasitemia, direct evidence linking these laboratory findings to field transmission dynamics is lacking. The manuscript appropriately frames these as possibilities ("may provide") rather than definitive solutions. Additional field studies would be needed to validate this hypothesis.

result: Based on Koch's historical data, an average blood parasitemia of 10-100 trypanosomes/ml can be calculated, meaning two or fewer trypanosomes would be present in an average tsetse bloodmeal.
evaluation: Claims C128-C129 are supported by calculations based on historical data from Koch (1909) presented in Appendix 1. Given that a tsetse bloodmeal is ~20 µl (C51), the arithmetic is straightforward. However, the accuracy depends on the reliability of Koch's century-old parasitemia estimates and whether they represent typical chronic infections. The calculation provides useful historical context but should be interpreted cautiously.

result: The essential biological function of the stumpy stage in T. brucei may be quorum sensing-dependent control of population size in the host rather than transmission. Density-dependent differentiation at the population level may be a later evolutionary innovation specific to the T. brucei group.
evaluation: Claims C153 and C156 represent speculative evolutionary interpretations. While the experimental data demonstrate that stumpy stage is not uniquely required for transmission (C118, C151), this does not definitively establish what the "essential" function is. The comparison to T. congolense (C152, C155) provides some comparative context, but evolutionary inferences require additional phylogenetic and functional data. These remain plausible hypotheses requiring further investigation.

result: Slender trypanosomes exhibit significantly higher motility than stumpy trypanosomes, and glucose levels are a developmental trigger in addition to cold shock and cis-aconitate.
evaluation: Claims C122-C123 cite established knowledge from the literature (Bargul et al., 2016; Qiu et al., 2018). These are not new findings from this study but provide important context for interpreting the results. The higher motility of slender cells (C122) is used to speculate about their higher TI values (discussion), though this hypothesis is not directly tested.

result: Stumpy cells have a limited lifespan (~3 days) and require at least one day to re-enter the cell cycle in the fly, meaning only young stumpy cells would be successful. The experiments used only freshly differentiated stumpy cells, thus overestimating their success rate under natural conditions.
evaluation: Claims C142-C147 combine established knowledge (C142: Turner et al., 1995) with findings from this study (C143: Figure 5C, 7C) and logical inferences (C144-C145, C147). The reasoning is sound: if stumpy cells live ~3 days and need 1 day to re-enter the cell cycle, then cells older than ~2 days would likely fail. The acknowledgment that experiments used fresh stumpy cells (C146) is an important limitation, suggesting the study may actually overestimate stumpy cell success in natural infections.

result: The lack of correlation between infective dose and midgut infections underlines the importance of the transmission index (TI) as a relative measure. What is biologically relevant is not the initiation of infection but the completion of the tsetse passage.
evaluation: Claims C78-C79 represent methodological and conceptual insights supported by the data patterns in Figure 2A. The observation that midgut infection rates vary inconsistently with dose while TI values show clearer patterns supports the interpretation that TI is a more meaningful metric. This is an important conceptual point for evaluating transmission competence, though the biological mechanisms underlying the dose-response patterns remain unclear.
